answer:
Viability is weak at this stage; the revenue path is plausible in principle but unvalidated, and several core assumptions are shaky.

Path to revenue: A per-restaurant monthly subscription ($50-$150) is a conventional, workable model, but the price is undecided and not anchored to any willingness-to-pay evidence. The only validation is that owners found the idea 'interesting,' which is not purchase intent. Unit economics are unquantified: at $100/month, customer acquisition via in-person visits, plus setup/POS integration and support, could easily exceed first-year revenue per customer, especially with a tiny ACV (~$1,200/yr). The projection of $24K in year one (20 customers) is arithmetic, not analysis; 'grows quickly' and 'profit by year three' have no supporting CAC, churn, or cost assumptions. Alternative monetization (revenue share, add-ons, multi-location) is speculative and distracts from proving the core.

Scalability: The 'software is scalable, margins very high' claim is overstated. POS integration is the hard part: dozens of fragmented POS systems, each requiring custom connectors and maintenance. Desktop installation implies per-site deployment, updates, support, and troubleshooting, which erodes software-like margins and slows growth. Selling one restaurant at a time through in-person visits to $100/month customers is a high-touch, low-ACV motion that does not scale well; the cited channels (associations, word of mouth) are unproven.

Assumption validity: (1) Market sizing is the 'if we get 1%' fallacy; no TAM/SAM defined, no count of the 15-60 table, wait-having segment. (2) The technical premise is untested: the model was trained on synthetic data plus one restaurant's sample, so predictive accuracy and its improvement over an experienced host are unknown. The status quo may be good enough, and the key risk is that accuracy gains do not translate to measurable revenue. Also, the model uses 'what guests ordered,' requiring real-time POS data, which contradicts the rationale of the offline desktop approach. (3) The desktop rationale (unreliable internet, data ownership) is asserted, not validated; most competitors are cloud-based and owners are accustomed to it, and desktop limits data network effects that would improve the model across customers. (4) Competitive differentiation is thin: incumbents (reservation/waitlist/POS vendors) already offer wait estimates and could add turn-time prediction cheaply; 'we do one thing well' is a feature, not a moat. Defensibility would have to come from proprietary data, which a desktop, siloed architecture undermines.

Team/execution risk: Student team with no industry advisor, no paying customers, no pilots, and no website. Relevant host experience is a plus, but go-to-market and enterprise-integration capability are unproven.

Strengths: Genuine, real pain point; clear target segment; working prototype; sensible plan to pilot with 5-10 restaurants and gather real data.

Bottom line: A reasonable hypothesis with a plausible but unproven business model. Next steps that would materially improve viability: run paid or LOI-backed pilots to test accuracy and willingness to pay, quantify the revenue/turn improvement per restaurant, define pricing and CAC/LTV, assess POS integration cost, and reconsider the desktop-versus-cloud architecture for data and scalability.
